Imagine a village of 512 people. Fields, bakeries, theatres, two banks. Everyone needs two loaves a month; three months without bread, and you die. Now imagine I build it twice, identical, and change one thing: where the money comes from. Then I run each village for ten years, ten times over, and count who still has bread.

In the first village money is what it is for us: it is born when a bank makes a loan, and every coin in your pocket is a coin someone else owes. In the second, everyone receives a fixed income every month — five units — and money that sits idle above a small cushion pays a parking fee: two percent a month simply disappears. Nobody owes anyone for it. That's the whole difference.

I don't switch everything on at once. Bare fields first. Then a government. A theatre. A stock market. Cooperatives. Taxes. One rung at a time, both villages, same rung, and at every rung: who is alive, what does bread cost, what does the government owe.

Bare fields, no government. In the debt village, a hundred and fifty-eight people are left after ten years. There is no work for most of them, without work no money, without money no bread. In the SuMSy village four hundred and fifty-eight live — and about twenty are hungry in any month: five units is half a meal, and half a meal keeps you alive only while someone hires you. Same fields, same bakers. Only the money, and who gets the work.

Add a government: public jobs and a bread allowance for the unemployed. Now almost everyone lives — and the government borrows half of what it spends, every month, for ten years, and never repays. Balance the books by taxing, and two hundred of five hundred and twelve are left. The debt village lives *because* its government goes into debt. And it can never get out: in that village, every coin in circulation is someone's debt.

It does — once. While the new money is still filling up the village, the parking tax brings in little, and the SuMSy government borrows its citizens' savings: about a month of guaranteed income per villager, at its worst in month six. Then it pays every unit back, by month thirty-three, in every run. A startup cost. One village repays; the other cannot. And from that step on, nobody in the SuMSy village is out of work — not one person, in ten years, in any run.

Now firms get owners, and shares that trade. In the debt village the gap between the richest tenth and the poorest is five hundred and seventy meals. In the SuMSy village, without a fee on land, it is ten thousand — and it is all land, hoarded because money melts and land doesn't. With the land fee paid out to everyone, two hundred and forty. With cooperatives, a hundred and sixty-six. The money system is not the whole story. Ownership is the other half, and land is a third.

Land. In the debt village a plot sells for thirty years of rent. In the SuMSy village, nobody sells — because money melts and land doesn't, so land becomes the thing to hold, and the rare sale goes for a fortune: seven hundred years of rent. Silvio Gesell saw this a century ago; his answer was for the state to buy the land out. Henry George's answer was a tax on land, and that's what the village tries: a fee on land, paid out to everyone as a dividend: then land trades again, at four years of rent, the dividend is larger than the income itself, and the poorest tenth of the village hold sixteen meals instead of one.

Then I did something unkind: I made everyone greedy. Spend every surplus, forever. The first time I ran it, the SuMSy village died — every run, every villager. It took three days to find out why, and it wasn't greed. The bakers planned on what their customers could afford instead of what they bought, and in a village where everyone has money, that meant buying three times the grain their ovens could bake. They went bankrupt with full storerooms while bread got cheaper. Fix the bakers' arithmetic and the greedy village feeds everyone, has the smallest gap of any village I built, and owes nothing. The debt village under the same greed lives too — on two hundred and thirty thousand of debt. The one thing that kills them both is panic: buyers who will pay double. No money survives that.

Ten years, ten runs, twelve rungs. What it takes to survive: in the debt village, a government willing to be permanently in debt, and a third of the village without work at every step. In the SuMSy village, an income everyone gets, a fee on idle money that pays for the state, a fee on land paid out as a dividend — and a labour market that shares the work, or the income alone leaves people behind. And a friend asked the question every banker will ask: give the debt village the same income and the same land dividend, and does it do as well? It does — everyone alive, nobody out of work — and it borrows three hundred and fifty thousand to do it. The income and the dividend keep a village alive in either money. What SuMSy adds is that nobody has to borrow them. In both: taxes that stay off bread — the one tax that killed the village was the tax on bread. And the open question I can't answer yet: what happens in the ten years when you switch from one money to the other. That's the next simulation.

Everything here is a rule I chose, and every number comes from a run you can repeat: the code, the village and the report are public. I built one village and broke it a hundred ways. The question I'd leave you with isn't which money is better. It's this: every rule of money is a choice someone made. Which of them would you change?
